captions: Hello, force scientists!
This is lesson 5.1: mass and weight.
Mass is the amount of matter, or stuff, in an object.
We measure mass in grams and kilograms, using a balance or scales.
A bag of rice has a mass of one kilogram, here, on the Moon, or anywhere.
The Earth pulls everything towards its centre. This pull is the force of gravity.
Weight is the force of gravity pulling on an object.
Because weight is a force, we measure it in newtons, using a forcemeter.
Pause and think. What unit do we use to measure weight?
A forcemeter has a spring inside.
Hang an object on the hook. The heavier it is, the more the spring stretches.
On Earth, an object with a mass of one kilogram weighs about ten newtons.
The Moon is much smaller than the Earth, so its gravity is weaker. It is about one sixth as strong.
An astronaut with a mass of sixty kilograms weighs about six hundred newtons on Earth.
On the Moon, her mass is still sixty kilograms, but she weighs only about one hundred newtons. That is why astronauts can bounce so high!
Your turn. On the Moon, what changes: your mass, or your weight?
Let's look for a pattern.
Measure the mass of some objects with a balance, and their weight with a forcemeter.
Record the results in a table.
You will find that every one hundred grams weighs about one newton.
Here is the pattern on a graph.
As the mass goes up, the weight goes up in the same way.
The more mass an object has, the more it weighs.
Let's remember.
Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms.
Weight is the pull of gravity, measured in newtons.
On Earth, one kilogram weighs about ten newtons.
And on the Moon your weight changes, but your mass does not.
Great work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Welcome back, force scientists!
This is lesson 5.2: the effects of forces.
A force is a push or a pull.
Forces can make things start moving, speed up, slow down or stop.
Forces can change the direction something moves, or change its shape, like squashing a ball of clay.
We draw forces as arrows.
The arrow points in the direction of the force.
A longer arrow shows a bigger force. Each arrow has a label, with the name of the force.
In a tug of war, both teams pull equally hard.
The forces are the same size but in opposite directions, so they are balanced.
The rope does not move. Balanced forces do not change the way something moves.
Now one team pulls harder.
The forces are unbalanced, so the rope starts moving towards the stronger team.
Unbalanced forces make things speed up, slow down or change direction.
Pause and think. What happens to a still object when the forces on it are balanced?
Friction acts between two surfaces that rub together. Rough surfaces make more friction.
Air resistance pushes against things moving through air. A parachute has a big surface to make lots of air resistance.
Water resistance pushes against things moving through water.
Your turn. Why does a parachute fall slowly?
Let's investigate friction.
Let a toy car roll down a ramp onto different surfaces: smooth wood, carpet and sandpaper.
Measure how far it rolls each time, keeping the ramp the same.
The rougher the surface, the more friction, and the shorter the distance.
Let's remember.
A force is a push or a pull.
We draw arrows to show the size and direction of forces.
Balanced forces cause no change, but unbalanced forces change how something moves.
And friction and air resistance slow things down.
Well done! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello again, force scientists!
This is lesson 5.3: floating and sinking.
Put a cork and a coin in water.
The cork floats, but the coin sinks to the bottom.
Why? Let's look at the forces.
An object in water has two forces on it.
Its weight pulls it down.
The water pushes it up. This upward push is called upthrust.
If the upthrust is as big as the weight, the object floats. If the weight is bigger, it sinks.
Pause and think. What is the name of the upward push of the water?
When an object goes into water, it pushes some water out of the way. We say it displaces the water.
The more water an object displaces, the bigger the upthrust.
That is why the water level in a bath rises when you get in!
A ball of clay sinks.
But if we shape the same clay into a boat, it floats!
The boat shape displaces much more water, so the upthrust is bigger.
This is how huge steel ships can float.
Your turn. Why does the clay float when it is shaped like a boat?
Let's investigate boat designs.
Make boats from the same foil, but with different base areas.
Add marbles one at a time, and count how many each boat holds before it sinks.
Then plot the results on a scatter graph and look for a pattern.
Here are the results on a scatter graph.
The bigger the base of the boat, the more marbles it can hold.
A wider boat displaces more water, so it gets more upthrust.
Let's remember.
Weight pulls down, and upthrust pushes up.
An object floats when the upthrust is as big as its weight.
Objects push water aside, or displace it.
And the shape of an object changes how much water it displaces.
Great job! See you in the practice room.

captions: Hello, electricity scientists!
This is lesson 5.4: different circuits and circuit diagrams.
Electricity flows only around a complete circuit.
A cell pushes the electricity around the wires and through the lamp.
If there is a gap anywhere, the circuit is broken and the lamp goes out.
Scientists draw circuits using simple symbols that everyone understands.
Here are the symbols for a cell, a battery, a lamp, a switch and a wire.
A drawing made with symbols is called a circuit diagram.
Pause and think. What do we call a drawing of a circuit made with symbols?
In a series circuit, everything is joined in one single loop.
If we add a second lamp in series, both lamps are dimmer.
And if one lamp breaks, the loop is broken, so the other lamp goes out too.
In a parallel circuit, each lamp has its own loop back to the cell.
The lamps stay bright.
And if one lamp breaks, the others stay on. That is why the lights in your home are wired in parallel.
Your turn. In which type of circuit do the other lamps stay on if one lamp breaks?
The push of a cell is called its voltage, measured in volts.
If we add more cells, the voltage goes up, and the lamp gets brighter.
But too many volts can make the lamp blow. Never use mains electricity for experiments!
Let's investigate voltage.
Build a circuit with one cell and one lamp, then add a second and a third cell.
Observe how bright the lamp is each time.
More cells give more voltage, so the lamp is brighter.
Let's remember.
A circuit must be complete for electricity to flow.
Circuit diagrams use symbols.
A series circuit has one loop, and a parallel circuit has separate loops.
And more cells give more voltage and brighter lamps.
Fantastic work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.
